Abstract:
Additive manufacturing (AM), or 3D printing, of metals is transforming the fabrication of components, in part by dramatically expanding the design space, allowing optimization of shape and topology. However, although the physical processes involved in AM are similar to those of welding, a field with decades of experimental, modeling, simulation, and characterization experience, qualification of AM parts remains a challenge. The availability of exascale computational systems, particularly when combined with data-driven approaches such as machine learning, enables topology and shape optimization as well as accelerated qualification by providing process-aware, locally accurate microstructure and mechanical property models. We describe the physics components comprising the Exascale Additive Manufacturing simulation environment and report progress using highly resolved melt pool simulations to inform part-scale finite element thermomechanics simulations, drive microstructure evolution, and determine constitutive mechanical property relationships based on those microstructures using polycrystal plasticity. We report on implementation of these components for exascale computing architectures, as well as the multi-stage simulation workflow that provides a unique high-fidelity model of process–structure–property relationships for AM parts. In addition, we discuss verification and validation through collaboration with efforts such as AM-Bench, a set of benchmark test problems under development by a team led by the National Institute of Standards and Technology.

Abstract:
An in-depth understanding of the texture formation in melt pools allows for the modification of the surface layer microstructure and corresponding material properties, providing an opportunity to integrate laser surface re-melting into metal additive manufacturing. This study investigates crystallographic texture formation at different cooling rates in single melting tracks on the Inconel 718 (IN718) plate produced by laser surface re-melting. The cooling rate varies from 2.31 × 105 °C/s to 9.56 × 105 °C/s with the increase in scanning rates from 400 mm/s to 1200 mm/s, measured by recently developed real-time temperature monitoring of melt pools. Columnar grains are dominant, with distinct crystallographic textures forming in the melt pools. At a slower scanning speed, the keyhole mode shows three different textures forming at different depths (crystallographically layered structure), while, at a faster scanning speed, the conduction mode shows only random grain orientation. There are no pores/voids detected, and the columnar grain morphology and columnar grain width (8.6 μm to 12.4 μm) follow the analysis framework in terms of thermal gradient and solidification rate analysis. This implies that laser surface re-melting provides the potential to modify the surface structure from a random grain orientation to a crystallographically layered structure.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This work presents an original surrogate model for the accurate and computationally efficient prediction of molten pool size in multi-track laser melting over a large domain at operating conditions relevant to laser powder bed fusion. While high-fidelity models can accurately predict the molten pool dynamics, the high computational expense limits their application to a few short tracks on small domains. Conduction models, on the other hand, are orders of magnitude cheaper to evaluate but lack the necessary physics for accurate predictions. This research presents a surrogate model that combines the computational efficiency of the conduction model with the accuracy of the high-fidelity model. A conduction model and high-fidelity model are simulated over a small scan pattern to generate training data of the highly transient molten pool depth and width. A data-driven model, consisting of a fuzzy basis function network, is trained with the aforementioned data. The conduction model is then simulated over a larger scan pattern, the results are input into the trained surrogate model, thereby outputting high-fidelity predictions of the molten pool size over a larger scan pattern. Comparison with experimental results shows this surrogate modeling framework provides reasonably accurate predictions of the molten pool depth and width (average error of -5.2% and 4.6%, respectively) and is a valid way to extend computationally intensive high-fidelity models to larger and more industrially relevant scan patterns.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) additive manufacturing, the melt pool (MP) characteristics are key indicators for process and part defects. For example, the laser scan location on the build plate can slightly change the MP size and shape due to the f-θ optics of the printer. The laser scan parameters can cause variations in MP signatures that may indicate lack-of-fusion and keyhole regimes. However, the effects of these process parameters on MP monitoring (MPM) signatures and part properties are not yet fully understood, especially during a multilayer big-part printing. In this study, our objective is to comprehensively evaluate the dynamical changes of MP signatures (location, intensity, size, and shape) under realistic printing scenarios-printing multilayer objects at different build plate locations with various print process settings. To accomplish this, we developed a coaxial high-speed camera-based MPM system for a commercial LPBF printer (EOS M290), to capture MP images continuously throughout a multilayer part. From our experimental data and results, we find that the MP image position on the camera sensor is not stationary as reported in the literature and is partly subjected to scan location. Its correlations to process deviation or part defect need to be determined. Also, the MP image profile can significantly reflect the changes in print process conditions. The developed system and analysis method can be used to establish a comprehensive profile of MP image signatures for online process diagnosis and part properties prediction, thus ensuring quality assurance and control in LPBF.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Achieving uniform melt-pool geometry in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) remains difficult due to nonlinear parameter interactions, stochastic powder-bed conditions, and progressive heat accumulation. These challenges are intensified by the lack of a sustainable digital manufacturing platform that can unify data, models, and control. To address this issue, this work introduces a unified LLM-agent-guided framework that integrates stochastic calibration and real-time control within a single pipeline. The work uses two coordinated agents. CalibAgent performs Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo calibration of an analytical thermal model of a multi-layer, and multi-track LPBF process using NIST AM-Bench melt-pool data, inferring distributions over absorptivity and thermal diffusivity. ControlAgent then uses the calibrated model to compute spatially varying laser-power schedules via analytical inversion, requiring no iterative optimization and executing in milliseconds. Demonstrations on IN718 across four scan geometries (horizontal and 45°cross-hatch, concentric triangular hatch, and a multi-layer L-shaped build) show that the controller reduces steady-state depth fluctuations by 83%-99% and eliminates turnaround spikes of up to 41 µm. In the multi-layer case, it maintains near-uniform depth across four layers without retraining or parameter adjustment. The framework requires no task-specific training, reward engineering, or expert tuning, enabling immediate extension to new materials and scan strategies.</jats:p>

Abstract:
A digital twin (DT) is a virtual representation of physical process, products and/or systems that requires a high-fidelity computational model for continuous update through the integration of sensor data and user input. In the context of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) additive manufacturing, a digital twin of the manufacturing process can offer predictions for the produced parts, diagnostics for manufacturing defects, as well as control capabilities. This paper introduces a parameterized physics-based digital twin (PPB-DT) for the statistical predictions of LPBF metal additive manufacturing process. We accomplish this by creating a high-fidelity computational model that accurately represents the melt pool phenomena and subsequently calibrating and validating it through controlled experiments. In PPB-DT, a mechanistic reduced-order method-driven stochastic calibration process is introduced, which enables the statistical predictions of the melt pool geometries and the identification of defects such as lack-of-fusion porosity and surface roughness, specifically for diagnostic applications. Leveraging data derived from this physics-based model and experiments, we have trained a machine learning-based digital twin (PPB-ML-DT) model for predicting, monitoring, and controlling melt pool geometries. These proposed digital twin models can be employed for predictions, control, optimization, and quality assurance within the LPBF process, ultimately expediting product development and certification in LPBF-based metal additive manufacturing.

{"answer": "## Porosity, Melt-Pool Depth, and Process Maps for LPBF 316L Stainless Steel: A Literature Benchmark for the Concept Laser M2 Parameter Window

### 1. Published 316L Process Maps and Density Data in the Proposed Window

The most directly comparable published study is the LLNL work by Kamath et al. (2014), who used a **Concept Laser M2** with a D4σ laser spot of **54 µm** (equivalent to Φ(99%) ≈ 81 µm) and 316L powder (CL20ES) at powers of **150–400 W**, 30 µm layers, and scan speeds spanning approximately 1200–2400 mm/s for density pillars (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000012). At 250 W and above, suitable scan speeds produced **>99% relative density**; at 400 W over 1900–2200 mm/s, density reached approximately **99.5%** (pqac-00000008). Density fell sharply at excessive speed (insufficient melting/LOF) and more gradually at low speed as keyhole voids formed (pqac-00000013). Single-track screening on the same M2 targeted melt-pool depths of **60–120 µm** (approximately 2–3× the 30 µm layer thickness) for high-density builds; the largest measured single-track depth was **195 µm** at 200 W and 500 mm/s (pqac-00000010). Note that the Kamath beam (54 µm D4σ) is considerably smaller than the user's production spot (130 µm), so the energy density at the same P and v is distributed over a larger area in the user's case, reducing penetration depth and shifting the keyhole and LOF boundaries.

Bateman et al. (2025) provide the **closest match to the user's exact machine and production parameters**: a GE Concept M2 with gas-atomized 316L (19–47 µm). Their standard/production condition used **370 W, 1350 mm/s, 90 µm hatch, 50 µm layer, and a 130 µm spot** (VED = 60.9 J/mm³), yielding porosity of **0.003–0.98%** across baseline and enhanced-spatter specimens (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043). Their low-energy condition (290 W, 1200 mm/s, 150 µm hatch, 50 µm layer, 50 µm spot; VED = 32.2 J/mm³) produced **5.85–8.60% porosity**, dominated by lack-of-fusion defects (pqac-00000041). Their high-energy condition (290 W, 800 mm/s, 70 µm hatch, 50 µm layer, 125 µm spot; VED = 103.6 J/mm³) yielded **0.55–1.82% porosity**, with both keyhole and LOF features reported (pqac-00000042). This demonstrates that even at higher VED, density did not necessarily improve, consistent with the onset of keyhole porosity.

Vallejo et al. (2021) used an **SLM 125HL** (≈70 µm spot, 100 °C preheat, argon, 30 µm layers, 120 µm hatch). Their optimized condition was **200 W, 800 mm/s** (VED = 69 J/mm³), achieving **99.89 ± 0.06% relative density**. The dense window spanned **46–127 J/mm³**, with ≥99.8% density throughout (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003). At 200 W, densities across scan speeds of 600–1400 mm/s were 99.92, 99.89, 99.88, 99.83, and 99.44%, respectively, illustrating the LOF edge near 40 J/mm³ (pqac-00000000). Melt-pool widths ranged from ~50–300 µm and depths from ~30–600 µm across all conditions (pqac-00000068).

Barrionuevo et al. (2024) used a **Concept Laser MLAB 200R** (≈80 µm spot, nitrogen, 30 µm layers) with 120–160 W and 700–1100 mm/s. The best densification was **98.3%** (Archimedes) or **99.70%** (image analysis) at 160 W, 700 mm/s, 40 µm hatch (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000044). At a supplementary 180 W point, density reached **99.41 ± 0.23%**; above 180 W, density fell below 98% due to overheating (pqac-00000007).

Yusuf et al. (2017) reported **Concept Laser M2** results at 200 W, 1600 mm/s, 50 µm layers: Archimedes density ≥99%, mean porosity ≈0.82%, XCT maximum porosity ≈0.61%, with spatially non-uniform pore distribution (pqac-00000051).

The following table summarizes these benchmark datasets:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2. Lack-of-Fusion Boundary

**Tang et al.'s geometric overlap criterion** is the most widely used LOF predictor. It models the melt pool as a half-ellipse and requires that adjacent tracks and layers overlap sufficiently. The criterion is expressed as **(H/W)² + (t/D)² ≤ 1**, where H is hatch spacing, W is melt-pool width, t is layer thickness, and D is melt-pool depth (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000026). When this sum exceeds unity, lack-of-fusion porosity is predicted. An alternative linear form, **t/D + H/W ≤ 1**, has also been used (pqac-00000023). Gordon et al. (2020) applied this criterion in Ti-6Al-4V defect structure process maps and noted that VED alone is not a robust LOF predictor because different H and t combinations at the same VED produce different overlap (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000063).

**In VED terms**, the LOF boundary for 316L at 30 µm layers and typical hatch spacings falls at approximately **40–50 J/mm³** (strongly supported). Vallejo et al. found ≥99.8% density for 46–127 J/mm³ (pqac-00000006), and density dropped to 99.44% at 39.7 J/mm³ and further at lower VED. Bateman et al.'s 32.2 J/mm³ condition (with a larger 150 µm hatch and 50 µm spot) produced 5.85–8.60% porosity (pqac-00000041), confirming that the LOF boundary is **sharp**: porosity can rise from <0.5% to >5% over a relatively narrow VED range once the melt pool no longer spans the hatch spacing or layer thickness.

**In P/v terms**, for the user's conditions (h = 0.09 mm, t = 0.03 mm), the LOF boundary corresponds to approximately P/v ≈ 0.12–0.14 J/mm (VED ≈ 44–52 J/mm³), though this depends on the actual melt-pool geometry at the specific spot size.

Smith et al. (2024) demonstrated that at a constant VED of 85 J/mm³ with a 100 µm spot on a DMP Flex 350, different P/v combinations produced different defect types and amounts, with low-P/low-v builds showing interpass LOF and high-P/high-v builds showing spatter-induced intrapass LOF (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048). This strongly supports the view that **VED is necessary but not sufficient** as a LOF predictor; the geometric criterion using actual melt-pool dimensions is more reliable.

Barrionuevo et al. recommended a VED above **125 J/mm³** for their Concept Laser MLAB (80 µm spot, 30 µm layers), which is significantly higher than Vallejo's 46 J/mm³ lower bound (pqac-00000007). This discrepancy likely reflects the smaller spot size (deeper, narrower pools) and different hatch spacing. This highlights that the LOF boundary is **machine- and spot-dependent** (weakly to moderately supported as a general principle; the specific numbers are machine-specific).

### 3. Keyhole Porosity Threshold for 316L at 50–130 µm Spots

King et al. (2014, LLNL) established the keyhole transition for 316L at a **normalized enthalpy ΔH/h_s ≈ 30 ± 4** using the definition ΔH/h_s = AP/(h_s √(π D_th v σ³)), where A is absorptivity (~0.4), h_s is the enthalpy at melting, D_th is thermal diffusivity, v is scan speed, and σ is the beam-radius parameter (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015). This threshold was validated with **both 52 µm and 130 µm D4σ beams**, confirming that it scales across beam sizes (pqac-00000059). The geometric keyhole criterion was **d > w/2** (depth exceeds half-width) (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000034).

Bertoli (2018, LLNL) derived a theoretical threshold of **ΔH/h_s ≈ 6** based on the energy to reach the boiling point: ΔH/h_s ≥ πT_b/T_m (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017). The difference between the theoretical ≈6 and experimental ≈30 reflects that the definitions differ (King's includes additional scaling factors) and that heat losses reduce effective enthalpy delivery.

Sabzi and Rivera-Díaz-del-Castillo (2019) reported that for 316L, normalized enthalpy values **above ~7** (using their definition) corresponded to keyhole formation, while below 7 was pore-free. At 200 W with scan speeds 850–1600 mm/s, pore fractions were 0.4–2.5% under keyhole conditions (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000057).

Forien et al. (2020, LLNL) identified the conduction-to-keyhole transition at ΔH/h ≈ **7.3** via in-situ pyrometry (pqac-00000018).

**Can 370 W at 1350 mm/s with a 130 µm spot keyhole?** Using King's formulation with the user's 130 µm D4σ spot (σ ≈ 32.5 µm), the normalized enthalpy at 370 W and 1350 mm/s evaluates to a value that falls **near or below** the keyhole threshold of 30 ± 4 (pqac-00000059). The larger beam distributes energy over a wider area, reducing peak intensity. For comparison, Gordon et al. noted a keyhole threshold surface power density of ~10⁶ W/cm² for Ti-6Al-4V; at 370 W over a 130 µm diameter circle, the irradiance is approximately **2.8 × 10⁶ W/cm²** (pqac-00000058), which could potentially induce keyhole behavior. However, the relatively high scan speed (1350 mm/s) limits the interaction time, reducing the likelihood of deep keyhole formation. Metelkova et al. (2018) showed that positive defocus (larger effective spot) generally retained conduction-mode processing over a wider parameter range (pqac-00000065), and that melt-pool depth was far more sensitive to beam size than width (pqac-00000064).

**Assessment (moderately supported):** The production condition (370 W, 1350 mm/s, 130 µm) likely operates in the **conduction-to-transition regime**, not deep keyhole. Keyhole porosity is more likely at slower scan speeds within the user's range (e.g., P/v > 0.4 J/mm at 130 µm spot). At the 50–70 µm contour spot and 100–120 W, the lower power keeps the system well within conduction mode.

### 4. Porosity and Melt-Pool Scatter / Repeatability

**Measurement repeatability:** Obeidi et al. (2021) reported a pycnometer measurement standard deviation of only **0.0002** (after 10 repeat measurements), with error bars of approximately **0.002** in relative density (pqac-00000050). Thus, the measurement method itself introduces negligible uncertainty.

**Within-condition scatter:** Vallejo et al. reported standard deviations on relative density ranging from **±0.05% to ±1.35%** across different parameter sets. At the optimum (200 W, 800 mm/s), the SD was only ±0.06%, while at suboptimal conditions (e.g., 125 W, 200 mm/s), it reached ±1.35% (pqac-00000000). This suggests that **scatter increases dramatically at marginal parameters** where stochastic defects (spatter, powder distribution irregularities) dominate.

**Spatter-induced variability:** Bateman et al. showed that at the standard 370 W/1350 mm/s condition, baseline porosity was **0.003%** while enhanced-spatter porosity reached **0.98%**—a variation of two orders of magnitude from spatter alone (pqac-00000040). The relative increase from spatter was 115% for standard energy, 22% for low energy, and 48% for high energy.

**Machine-to-machine variability:** Obeidi et al. found that four machines with the same powder and nominal parameters produced densities spanning approximately **93.88–97.67%** (a ~4 percentage-point range), with Aconity and EOS M280 performing best and Concept Laser (nitrogen atmosphere) performing worst (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000054). Contributing factors included build-chamber size, gas flow, recoater design, and gas type (pqac-00000053).

**Implications for the user's comb specimens (weakly supported, extrapolated):** No study was found reporting direct wall-to-wall porosity scatter for thin-wall geometries. However, based on the above data, for well-optimized parameters (VED ~50–100 J/mm³), wall-to-wall porosity differences below **~0.1–0.3 percentage points** may be within normal stochastic scatter, while differences exceeding **~0.5 percentage points** likely reflect a real process-parameter effect. At marginal parameters near the LOF boundary, scatter increases substantially.

### 5. Open Datasets for Comparison

**LLNL Keyhole-Mode Microscopy Dataset** (Ahlquist et al. 2022, DOE OSTI ID 1878448, DOI: 10.2172/1878448): Contains single-track cross-sectional images, melt-pool width, depth, height, contact angles, continuity ratings, and cavity locations/contours from LPBF experiments. CSV/Excel files are indexed by plate and track. Directly relevant for keyhole-mode benchmarking (pqac-00000029).

**MeltpoolNet** (Akbari et al.): A tabular dataset of metallic AM melt-pool characteristics referenced in multiple ML studies (pqac-00000030). It aggregates process parameters and melt-pool dimensions across alloys including 316L, though the depth of 316L coverage varies.

**Melt-Pool-Kinetics** (Jabbour et al. 2025, Figshare, DOI: 10.1038/s41597-025-05597-2): A multi-source compilation in HDF5 format with metadata covering AM process, material, laser power, scan speed, beam size, layer thickness, and defect results. A metadata spreadsheet enables filtering for LPBF 316L entries (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031).

**NIST AM-Bench** (2018, 2022, 2025 challenges): Primarily focused on **IN718** and **IN625** single-track and multi-layer builds with carefully controlled melt-pool measurements. The 316L coverage is limited; the benchmark's main value for the user is methodological rather than material-specific (pqac-00000031).

**Journal supplementary data:** Vallejo et al. (2021) Table 1 contains a full parameter-density matrix for 316L on the SLM 125HL (pqac-00000000). Barrionuevo et al. (2024) Table 1 compiles a literature survey of 316L LPBF parameters and densities across >10 machines (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000049). Gordon et al. (2020) provide Ti-6Al-4V defect process maps with XCT-derived porosity data that can serve as a cross-material reference for the Tang criterion (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000063).

### 6. Summary of Key Thresholds and Recommendations

**Lack-of-fusion boundary (316L, 30 µm layers, 0.09 mm hatch, 100–130 µm spot):**
- VED: approximately **40–50 J/mm³** (strongly supported by multiple studies)
- P/v: approximately **0.11–0.14 J/mm** (dependent on spot and hatch)
- Tang criterion: **(H/W)² + (t/D)² < 1**; this requires knowing W and D at each condition

**Keyhole boundary (316L, 130 µm spot):**
- King's normalized enthalpy: **ΔH/h_s ≈ 30 ± 4** (strongly supported, validated at both 52 and 130 µm)
- Geometric criterion: **d/w > 0.5** or depth exceeding half-width
- At 370 W / 1350 mm/s / 130 µm: likely **conduction-to-transition mode**, not deep keyhole (moderately supported)
- Keyhole risk increases at slower speeds (P/v > ~0.4–0.5 J/mm at 130 µm)

**Expected porosity across the user's window (P = 150–370 W, v ≈ 335–2930 mm/s, h = 0.09 mm, t = 30 µm, 130 µm spot):**
- VED range: ~33–204 J/mm³
- At 33–45 J/mm³ (high-v / low-P corner): **>1–8% porosity** from LOF (pqac-00000041)
- At 50–130 J/mm³ (central window): **<0.5% porosity**, potentially <0.1% at optimum (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000040)
- At >130–200 J/mm³ (low-v / high-P corner): porosity may rise to **0.5–2%** from keyhole and overheating effects (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000006)

**Melt-pool depth estimates:** At the production condition (370 W, 1350 mm/s, 130 µm spot), Kamath et al.'s single-track screening targeted **60–120 µm** depth for high-density builds with a 54 µm beam (pqac-00000010). With the larger 130 µm spot, shallower pools are expected at the same P/v. At slow speeds (e.g., 370 W, 335 mm/s), depths could reach **200+ µm**, potentially entering keyhole territory.

### Key References with DOIs

1. **Kamath et al. (2014)**, *Int J Adv Manuf Technol* 74:65–78, DOI: 10.1007/s00170-014-5954-9 — Concept Laser M2, 316L density at 150–400 W
2. **King et al. (2014)**, *J Mater Process Technol* 214:2915–2925, DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2014.06.005 — Keyhole observation, ΔH/h_s ≈ 30 ± 4, both 52 and 130 µm beams
3. **Bertoli et al. (2017)**, *Mater Des* 113:331–340, DOI: 10.1016/j.matdes.2016.10.037 — Limitations of VED, single-track 316L, normalized enthalpy
4. **Ye et al. (2019)**, *Adv Eng Mater* 21(7), DOI: 10.1002/adem.201900185 — Absorptivity and melt-pool depth scaling for 316L
5. **Vallejo et al. (2021)**, *Metals* 11:832, DOI: 10.3390/met11050832 — 316L process optimization, 46–127 J/mm³ dense window
6. **Bateman et al. (2025)**, preprint, DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-7687521/v1 — GE Concept M2, 370 W/1350 mm/s/130 µm production parameters
7. **Obeidi et al. (2021)**, *J Mater Res Technol* 13:2361–2374, DOI: 10.1016/j.jmrt.2021.06.027 — Multi-machine 316L comparison
8. **Gordon et al. (2020)**, *Addit Manuf* 36:101552, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2020.101552 — Defect structure process maps, Tang LOF criterion
9. **Smith et al. (2024)**, *JOM* 77:737–748, DOI: 10.1007/s11837-024-06946-z — VED limitations, modified LOF criteria for 316L
10. **Sabzi & Rivera-Díaz-del-Castillo (2019)**, *Materials* 12:3791, DOI: 10.3390/ma12223791 — Defect prevention model for 316L
11. **Tang et al. (2017)**, *Addit Manuf* 14:39–48, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2016.12.001 — LOF porosity prediction geometric criterion
12. **Metelkova et al. (2018)**, *Addit Manuf* 23:161–169, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2018.08.006 — Defocusing effects on 316L melt pools

### 1. Published 316L Process Maps and Density Data in the Proposed Window

The most directly comparable published study is the LLNL work by Kamath et al. (2014), who used a **Concept Laser M2** with a D4σ laser spot of **54 µm** (equivalent to Φ(99%) ≈ 81 µm) and 316L powder (CL20ES) at powers of **150–400 W**, 30 µm layers, and scan speeds spanning approximately 1200–2400 mm/s for density pillars (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000012). Single-track screening on the same M2 targeted melt-pool depths of **60–120 µm** (approximately 2–3× the 30 µm layer thickness) for high-density builds; the largest measured single-track depth was **195 µm** at 200 W and 500 mm/s (pqac-00000010). The best densification was **98.3%** (Archimedes) or **99.70%** (image analysis) at 160 W, 700 mm/s, 40 µm hatch (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000044). At a supplementary 180 W point, density reached **99.41 ± 0.23%**; above 180 W, density fell below 98% due to overheating (pqac-00000007).

Yusuf et al. (2017) reported **Concept Laser M2** results at 200 W, 1600 mm/s, 50 µm layers: Archimedes density ≥99%, mean porosity ≈0.82%, XCT maximum porosity ≈0.61%, with spatially non-uniform pore distribution (pqac-00000051).

The following table summarizes these benchmark datasets:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2. Lack-of-Fusion Boundary

**Tang et al.'s geometric overlap criterion** is the most widely used LOF predictor. It models the melt pool as a half-ellipse and requires that adjacent tracks and layers overlap sufficiently. The criterion is expressed as **(H/W)² + (t/D)² ≤ 1**, where H is hatch spacing, W is melt-pool width, t is layer thickness, and D is melt-pool depth (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000026). When this sum exceeds unity, lack-of-fusion porosity is predicted. An alternative linear form, **t/D + H/W ≤ 1**, has also been used (pqac-00000023). Gordon et al. (2020) applied this criterion in Ti-6Al-4V defect structure process maps and noted that VED alone is not a robust LOF predictor because different H and t combinations at the same VED produce different overlap (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000063).

**In VED terms**, the LOF boundary for 316L at 30 µm layers and typical hatch spacings falls at approximately **40–50 J/mm³** (strongly supported). Vallejo et al. found ≥99.8% density for 46–127 J/mm³ (pqac-00000006), and density dropped to 99.44% at 39.7 J/mm³ and further at lower VED. Bateman et al.'s 32.2 J/mm³ condition (with a larger 150 µm hatch and 50 µm spot) produced 5.85–8.60% porosity (pqac-00000041), confirming that the LOF boundary is **sharp**: porosity can rise from <0.5% to >5% over a relatively narrow VED range once the melt pool no longer spans the hatch spacing or layer thickness.

**In P/v terms**, for the user's conditions (h = 0.09 mm, t = 0.03 mm), the LOF boundary corresponds to approximately P/v ≈ 0.12–0.14 J/mm (VED ≈ 44–52 J/mm³), though this depends on the actual melt-pool geometry at the specific spot size.

Smith et al. (2024) demonstrated that at a constant VED of 85 J/mm³ with a 100 µm spot on a DMP Flex 350, different P/v combinations produced different defect types and amounts, with low-P/low-v builds showing interpass LOF and high-P/high-v builds showing spatter-induced intrapass LOF (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048). This strongly supports the view that **VED is necessary but not sufficient** as a LOF predictor; the geometric criterion using actual melt-pool dimensions is more reliable.

Barrionuevo et al. recommended a VED above **125 J/mm³** for their Concept Laser MLAB (80 µm spot, 30 µm layers), which is significantly higher than Vallejo's 46 J/mm³ lower bound (pqac-00000007). This discrepancy likely reflects the smaller spot size (deeper, narrower pools) and different hatch spacing. This highlights that the LOF boundary is **machine- and spot-dependent** (weakly to moderately supported as a general principle; the specific numbers are machine-specific).

### 3. Keyhole Porosity Threshold for 316L at 50–130 µm Spots

King et al. (2014, LLNL) established the keyhole transition for 316L at a **normalized enthalpy ΔH/h_s ≈ 30 ± 4** using the definition ΔH/h_s = AP/(h_s √(π D_th v σ³)), where A is absorptivity (~0.4), h_s is the enthalpy at melting, D_th is thermal diffusivity, v is scan speed, and σ is the beam-radius parameter (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015). This threshold was validated with **both 52 µm and 130 µm D4σ beams**, confirming that it scales across beam sizes (pqac-00000059). The geometric keyhole criterion was **d > w/2** (depth exceeds half-width) (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000034).

Bertoli (2018, LLNL) derived a theoretical threshold of **ΔH/h_s ≈ 6** based on the energy to reach the boiling point: ΔH/h_s ≥ πT_b/T_m (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017). The difference between the theoretical ≈6 and experimental ≈30 reflects that the definitions differ (King's includes additional scaling factors) and that heat losses reduce effective enthalpy delivery.

Sabzi and Rivera-Díaz-del-Castillo (2019) reported that for 316L, normalized enthalpy values **above ~7** (using their definition) corresponded to keyhole formation, while below 7 was pore-free. At 200 W with scan speeds 850–1600 mm/s, pore fractions were 0.4–2.5% under keyhole conditions (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000057).

Forien et al. (2020, LLNL) identified the conduction-to-keyhole transition at ΔH/h ≈ **7.3** via in-situ pyrometry (pqac-00000018).

**Can 370 W at 1350 mm/s with a 130 µm spot keyhole?** Using King's formulation with the user's 130 µm D4σ spot (σ ≈ 32.5 µm), the normalized enthalpy at 370 W and 1350 mm/s evaluates to a value that falls **near or below** the keyhole threshold of 30 ± 4 (pqac-00000059). The larger beam distributes energy over a wider area, reducing peak intensity. For comparison, Gordon et al. noted a keyhole threshold surface power density of ~10⁶ W/cm² for Ti-6Al-4V; at 370 W over a 130 µm diameter circle, the irradiance is approximately **2.8 × 10⁶ W/cm²** (pqac-00000058), which could potentially induce keyhole behavior. However, the relatively high scan speed (1350 mm/s) limits the interaction time, reducing the likelihood of deep keyhole formation. Metelkova et al. (2018) showed that positive defocus (larger effective spot) generally retained conduction-mode processing over a wider parameter range (pqac-00000065), and that melt-pool depth was far more sensitive to beam size than width (pqac-00000064).

**Assessment (moderately supported):** The production condition (370 W, 1350 mm/s, 130 µm) likely operates in the **conduction-to-transition regime**, not deep keyhole. Keyhole porosity is more likely at slower scan speeds within the user's range (e.g., P/v > 0.4 J/mm at 130 µm spot). At the 50–70 µm contour spot and 100–120 W, the lower power keeps the system well within conduction mode.

### 4. Porosity and Melt-Pool Scatter / Repeatability

**Measurement repeatability:** Obeidi et al. (2021) reported a pycnometer measurement standard deviation of only **0.0002** (after 10 repeat measurements), with error bars of approximately **0.002** in relative density (pqac-00000050). Thus, the measurement method itself introduces negligible uncertainty.

**Within-condition scatter:** Vallejo et al. reported standard deviations on relative density ranging from **±0.05% to ±1.35%** across different parameter sets. At the optimum (200 W, 800 mm/s), the SD was only ±0.06%, while at suboptimal conditions (e.g., 125 W, 200 mm/s), it reached ±1.35% (pqac-00000000). This suggests that **scatter increases dramatically at marginal parameters** where stochastic defects (spatter, powder distribution irregularities) dominate.

**Spatter-induced variability:** Bateman et al. showed that at the standard 370 W/1350 mm/s condition, baseline porosity was **0.003%** while enhanced-spatter porosity reached **0.98%**—a variation of two orders of magnitude from spatter alone (pqac-00000040). The relative increase from spatter was 115% for standard energy, 22% for low energy, and 48% for high energy.

**Machine-to-machine variability:** Obeidi et al. found that four machines with the same powder and nominal parameters produced densities spanning approximately **93.88–97.67%** (a ~4 percentage-point range), with Aconity and EOS M280 performing best and Concept Laser (nitrogen atmosphere) performing worst (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000054). Contributing factors included build-chamber size, gas flow, recoater design, and gas type (pqac-00000053).

**Implications for the user's comb specimens (weakly supported, extrapolated):** No study was found reporting direct wall-to-wall porosity scatter for thin-wall geometries. However, based on the above data, for well-optimized parameters (VED ~50–100 J/mm³), wall-to-wall porosity differences below **~0.1–0.3 percentage points** may be within normal stochastic scatter, while differences exceeding **~0.5 percentage points** likely reflect a real process-parameter effect. At marginal parameters near the LOF boundary, scatter increases substantially.

### 5. Open Datasets for Comparison

**LLNL Keyhole-Mode Microscopy Dataset** (Ahlquist et al. 2022, DOE OSTI ID 1878448, DOI: 10.2172/1878448): Contains single-track cross-sectional images, melt-pool width, depth, height, contact angles, continuity ratings, and cavity locations/contours from LPBF experiments. CSV/Excel files are indexed by plate and track. Directly relevant for keyhole-mode benchmarking (pqac-00000029).

**MeltpoolNet** (Akbari et al.): A tabular dataset of metallic AM melt-pool characteristics referenced in multiple ML studies (pqac-00000030). It aggregates process parameters and melt-pool dimensions across alloys including 316L, though the depth of 316L coverage varies.

**Melt-Pool-Kinetics** (Jabbour et al. 2025, Figshare, DOI: 10.1038/s41597-025-05597-2): A multi-source compilation in HDF5 format with metadata covering AM process, material, laser power, scan speed, beam size, layer thickness, and defect results. A metadata spreadsheet enables filtering for LPBF 316L entries (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031).

**NIST AM-Bench** (2018, 2022, 2025 challenges): Primarily focused on **IN718** and **IN625** single-track and multi-layer builds with carefully controlled melt-pool measurements. The 316L coverage is limited; the benchmark's main value for the user is methodological rather than material-specific (pqac-00000031).

**Journal supplementary data:** Vallejo et al. (2021) Table 1 contains a full parameter-density matrix for 316L on the SLM 125HL (pqac-00000000). Barrionuevo et al. (2024) Table 1 compiles a literature survey of 316L LPBF parameters and densities across >10 machines (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000049). Gordon et al. (2020) provide Ti-6Al-4V defect process maps with XCT-derived porosity data that can serve as a cross-material reference for the Tang criterion (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000063).

### 6. Summary of Key Thresholds and Recommendations

**Lack-of-fusion boundary (316L, 30 µm layers, 0.09 mm hatch, 100–130 µm spot):**
- VED: approximately **40–50 J/mm³** (strongly supported by multiple studies)
- P/v: approximately **0.11–0.14 J/mm** (dependent on spot and hatch)
- Tang criterion: **(H/W)² + (t/D)² < 1**; this requires knowing W and D at each condition

**Keyhole boundary (316L, 130 µm spot):**
- King's normalized enthalpy: **ΔH/h_s ≈ 30 ± 4** (strongly supported, validated at both 52 and 130 µm)
- Geometric criterion: **d/w > 0.5** or depth exceeding half-width
- At 370 W / 1350 mm/s / 130 µm: likely **conduction-to-transition mode**, not deep keyhole (moderately supported)
- Keyhole risk increases at slower speeds (P/v > ~0.4–0.5 J/mm at 130 µm)

**Expected porosity across the user's window (P = 150–370 W, v ≈ 335–2930 mm/s, h = 0.09 mm, t = 30 µm, 130 µm spot):**
- VED range: ~33–204 J/mm³
- At 33–45 J/mm³ (high-v / low-P corner): **>1–8% porosity** from LOF (pqac-00000041)
- At 50–130 J/mm³ (central window): **<0.5% porosity**, potentially <0.1% at optimum (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000040)
- At >130–200 J/mm³ (low-v / high-P corner): porosity may rise to **0.5–2%** from keyhole and overheating effects (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000006)

**Melt-pool depth estimates:** At the production condition (370 W, 1350 mm/s, 130 µm spot), Kamath et al.'s single-track screening targeted **60–120 µm** depth for high-density builds with a 54 µm beam (pqac-00000010). With the larger 130 µm spot, shallower pools are expected at the same P/v. At slow speeds (e.g., 370 W, 335 mm/s), depths could reach **200+ µm**, potentially entering keyhole territory.

### Key References with DOIs

1. **Kamath et al. (2014)**, *Int J Adv Manuf Technol* 74:65–78, DOI: 10.1007/s00170-014-5954-9 — Concept Laser M2, 316L density at 150–400 W
2. **King et al. (2014)**, *J Mater Process Technol* 214:2915–2925, DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2014.06.005 — Keyhole observation, ΔH/h_s ≈ 30 ± 4, both 52 and 130 µm beams
3. **Bertoli et al. (2017)**, *Mater Des* 113:331–340, DOI: 10.1016/j.matdes.2016.10.037 — Limitations of VED, single-track 316L, normalized enthalpy
4. **Ye et al. (2019)**, *Adv Eng Mater* 21(7), DOI: 10.1002/adem.201900185 — Absorptivity and melt-pool depth scaling for 316L
5. **Vallejo et al. (2021)**, *Metals* 11:832, DOI: 10.3390/met11050832 — 316L process optimization, 46–127 J/mm³ dense window
6. **Bateman et al. (2025)**, preprint, DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-7687521/v1 — GE Concept M2, 370 W/1350 mm/s/130 µm production parameters
7. **Obeidi et al. (2021)**, *J Mater Res Technol* 13:2361–2374, DOI: 10.1016/j.jmrt.2021.06.027 — Multi-machine 316L comparison
8. **Gordon et al. (2020)**, *Addit Manuf* 36:101552, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2020.101552 — Defect structure process maps, Tang LOF criterion
9. **Smith et al. (2024)**, *JOM* 77:737–748, DOI: 10.1007/s11837-024-06946-z — VED limitations, modified LOF criteria for 316L
10. **Sabzi & Rivera-Díaz-del-Castillo (2019)**, *Materials* 12:3791, DOI: 10.3390/ma12223791 — Defect prevention model for 316L
11. **Tang et al. (2017)**, *Addit Manuf* 14:39–48, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2016.12.001 — LOF porosity prediction geometric criterion
12. **Metelkova et al. (2018)**, *Addit Manuf* 23:161–169, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2018.08.006 — Defocusing effects on 316L melt pools
13. **Barrionuevo et al. (2024)**, *J Manuf Mater Process* 8:35, DOI: 10.3390/jmmp8010035 — 316L on Concept Laser MLAB, literature compilation

state.question:
What porosity (or relative density) and melt-pool depth should we expect from LPBF 316L stainless steel across laser power 150-370 W and scan speed 335-2930 mm/s with a 100-130 um spot and 0.09 mm hatch spacing, and which published measurements and process maps can our results be compared against? Context: laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M, L-PBF) of commercial gas-atomized 316L stainless steel powder (about 15-45 um) on a Concept Laser M2 cusing (CL WRX Control 2.4; two 400 W class continuous-wave Yb fibre lasers at about 1070 nm, only one used; galvanometer scanner; nitrogen or argon; no plate heating; layer thickness 30 or 50 um, not yet confirmed). The machine's production 316L parameter set uses, for the core hatch, 370 W, 1350 mm/s, 0.09 mm hatch spacing and a 130 um spot (P/v = 0.274 J/mm), contours at 100-120 W and 130-220 mm/s with a 50-70 um spot, and an upskin at 200 W, 980 mm/s, 0.075 mm hatch. The build: 12 'comb' parts, each a 44.5 x 12.7 mm base (printed with the production set) carrying 7 thin walls (fins) 1.27 mm thick, 12.7 mm long and 7.6 mm tall on a 7.2 mm pitch. Every wall has its own core and upskin laser power P and scan speed v (contours unchanged): 60 settings from a scrambled Sobol sequence over P = 150-370 W and P/v = 0.09-0.55 J/mm (v about 335-2930 mm/s; about 33-204 J/mm^3 at 30 um layers), plus the production hatch as a control. Three parts stand on each of four removable 88 mm square 316L panels; the fourth panel is turned 90 degrees so its walls run across the recoater instead of along it, and repeats 18 settings and the control, giving 21 pairs printed in both orientations. After the build each part is cut lengthwise near its centreline and between walls 4 and 5, hot-mounted in 1.25 in conductive mounts, ground to the centreline (a section through every wall's thickness and height at mid-length), polished, imaged unetched in an SEM (Thermo Fisher Apreo C) for porosity in each wall's core (at least 0.2 mm from the faces, 1 mm from the base and the top), then etched to reveal the last layer's melt-pool boundaries. The results will be compared with the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing (AM) Module (CALPHAD-based properties; steady-state and transient melt-pool calculations; printability maps of lack of fusion, keyholing and balling), to calibrate and test it, and later builds will choose settings by batch Bayesian optimization.

Answer with citations and DOIs. Quote numbers with the conditions they apply to (material, P, v, spot size and how it was defined, hatch spacing, layer thickness, machine, gas). Prefer primary sources, say where sources disagree, and flag which statements are strongly versus weakly supported. Where a paper gives a data table or an open dataset we could compare against, say exactly where (table or figure number, repository and identifier).

In particular:
1. Published 316L process maps and density data in or near this window, especially from Concept Laser M2 machines (for example the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory work: density of 316L at powers up to 400 W, keyhole-mode melting, and the related single-track and Eagar-Tsai/normalized-enthalpy analyses), and from other machines with a similar spot (EOS M280/M290, SLM 280, Renishaw). Give the P, v, h, t, spot and the measured density or porosity, and where the lack-of-fusion and keyhole boundaries fell.
2. Where the lack-of-fusion boundary sits in volumetric energy density, in P/v, and in dimensionless terms (normalized enthalpy dH/h_s, keyhole number, Tang et al.'s overlap criterion); how sharp it is; and how porosity rises below it.
3. Where keyhole porosity starts for 316L at spots of 50-130 um, and whether a 130 um spot at up to 370 W can keyhole at all at these speeds.
4. How much porosity and melt-pool depth scatter between nominally identical specimens or positions on the plate (repeatability), so we know what difference between two walls is real.
5. Open datasets (MeltpoolNet, NIST, LLNL, Zenodo, Materials Data Facility, Mendeley Data, journal supplements) with 316L P, v, spot, hatch, layer and porosity or melt-pool dimensions.

## Porosity, Melt-Pool Depth, and Process Maps for LPBF 316L Stainless Steel: A Literature Benchmark for the Concept Laser M2 Parameter Window

### 1. Published 316L Process Maps and Density Data in the Proposed Window

The most directly comparable published study is the LLNL work by Kamath et al. (2014), who used a **Concept Laser M2** with a D4σ laser spot of **54 µm** (equivalent to Φ(99%) ≈ 81 µm) and 316L powder (CL20ES) at powers of **150–400 W**, 30 µm layers, and scan speeds spanning approximately 1200–2400 mm/s for density pillars (kamath2014densityofadditivelymanufactured pages 1-5, kamath2014densityofadditivelymanufactured pages 5-7). At 250 W and above, suitable scan speeds produced **>99% relative density**; at 400 W over 1900–2200 mm/s, density reached approximately **99.5%** (kamath2014densityofadditivelymanufactured pages 13-16). Density fell sharply at excessive speed (insufficient melting/LOF) and more gradually at low speed as keyhole voids formed (kamath2014densityofadditivelymanufactured pages 1-5). Single-track screening on the same M2 targeted melt-pool depths of **60–120 µm** (approximately 2–3× the 30 µm layer thickness) for high-density builds; the largest measured single-track depth was **195 µm** at 200 W and 500 mm/s (kamath2014densityofadditivelymanufactured pages 9-13). Note that the Kamath beam (54 µm D4σ) is considerably smaller than the user's production spot (130 µm), so the energy density at the same P and v is distributed over a larger area in the user's case, reducing penetration depth and shifting the keyhole and LOF boundaries.

Bateman et al. (2025) provide the **closest match to the user's exact machine and production parameters**: a GE Concept M2 with gas-atomized 316L (19–47 µm). Their standard/production condition used **370 W, 1350 mm/s, 90 µm hatch, 50 µm layer, and a 130 µm spot** (VED = 60.9 J/mm³), yielding porosity of **0.003–0.98%** across baseline and enhanced-spatter specimens (bateman2025effectsoflpbf pages 6-13, bateman2025effectsoflpbf pages 1-6). Their low-energy condition (290 W, 1200 mm/s, 150 µm hatch, 50 µm layer, 50 µm spot; VED = 32.2 J/mm³) produced **5.85–8.60% porosity**, dominated by lack-of-fusion defects (bateman2025effectsoflpbf pages 6-13). Their high-energy condition (290 W, 800 mm/s, 70 µm hatch, 50 µm layer, 125 µm spot; VED = 103.6 J/mm³) yielded **0.55–1.82% porosity**, with both keyhole and LOF features reported (bateman2025effectsoflpbf pages 13-18). This demonstrates that even at higher VED, density did not necessarily improve, consistent with the onset of keyhole porosity.

Vallejo et al. (2021) used an **SLM 125HL** (≈70 µm spot, 100 °C preheat, argon, 30 µm layers, 120 µm hatch). Their optimized condition was **200 W, 800 mm/s** (VED = 69 J/mm³), achieving **99.89 ± 0.06% relative density**. The dense window spanned **46–127 J/mm³**, with ≥99.8% density throughout (vallejo2021processoptimizationand pages 2-4, vallejo2021processoptimizationand pages 1-2). At 200 W, densities across scan speeds of 600–1400 mm/s were 99.92, 99.89, 99.88, 99.83, and 99.44%, respectively, illustrating the LOF edge near 40 J/mm³ (vallejo2021processoptimizationand pages 2-4). Melt-pool widths ranged from ~50–300 µm and depths from ~30–600 µm across all conditions (vallejo2021processoptimizationand pages 13-14).

Barrionuevo et al. (2024) used a **Concept Laser MLAB 200R** (≈80 µm spot, nitrogen, 30 µm layers) with 120–160 W and 700–1100 mm/s. The best densification was **98.3%** (Archimedes) or **99.70%** (image analysis) at 160 W, 700 mm/s, 40 µm hatch (barrionuevo2024influenceofthe pages 4-6). At a supplementary 180 W point, density reached **99.41 ± 0.23%**; above 180 W, density fell below 98% due to overheating (barrionuevo2024influenceofthe pages 11-14).

Yusuf et al. (2017) reported **Concept Laser M2** results at 200 W, 1600 mm/s, 50 µm layers: Archimedes density ≥99%, mean porosity ≈0.82%, XCT maximum porosity ≈0.61%, with spatially non-uniform pore distribution (yusuf2017investigationonporosity pages 1-3).

The following table summarizes these benchmark datasets:

(2014), DOI: [10.1007/s00170-014-5954-9](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-014-5954-9) | Concept Laser M2 | 54 µm, **D4σ**; also reported as 81 µm Φ(99%) | 150–400 | ≈1200–2400 for density pillars | Nominal track width 150; hatch not explicitly recovered | 30 | Not reported consistently | At ≥250 W, suitable speeds gave **>99% relative density**; at 400 W and 1900–2200 mm/s, ≈**99.5% relative density** | Not established in recovered density passage | Closest foundational M2 study, but its 54 µm D4σ beam is much smaller than the proposed 100–130 µm spot. *Table: Published LPBF 316L density and porosity measurements closest to the proposed Concept Laser M2 parameter window. The table preserves beam-definition and atmosphere caveats because nominally similar energy inputs are not directly comparable across machines.*

### 2. Lack-of-Fusion Boundary

**Tang et al.'s geometric overlap criterion** is the most widely used LOF predictor. It models the melt pool as a half-ellipse and requires that adjacent tracks and layers overlap sufficiently. The criterion is expressed as **(H/W)² + (t/D)² ≤ 1**, where H is hatch spacing, W is melt-pool width, t is layer thickness, and D is melt-pool depth (harkin2023evaluationofthe pages 2-3, gordon2020defectstructureprocess pages 3-4). When this sum exceeds unity, lack-of-fusion porosity is predicted. An alternative linear form, **t/D + H/W ≤ 1**, has also been used (subraveti2024threedimensionalpredictionof pages 1-4). Gordon et al. (2020) applied this criterion in Ti-6Al-4V defect structure process maps and noted that VED alone is not a robust LOF predictor because different H and t combinations at the same VED produce different overlap (gordon2020defectstructureprocess pages 3-4, gordon2020defectstructureprocess pages 1-2).

**In VED terms**, the LOF boundary for 316L at 30 µm layers and typical hatch spacings falls at approximately **40–50 J/mm³** (strongly supported). Vallejo et al. found ≥99.8% density for 46–127 J/mm³ (vallejo2021processoptimizationand pages 16-18), and density dropped to 99.44% at 39.7 J/mm³ and further at lower VED. Bateman et al.'s 32.2 J/mm³ condition (with a larger 150 µm hatch and 50 µm spot) produced 5.85–8.60% porosity (bateman2025effectsoflpbf pages 6-13), confirming that the LOF boundary is **sharp**: porosity can rise from <0.5% to >5% over a relatively narrow VED range once the melt pool no longer spans the hatch spacing or layer thickness.

**In P/v terms**, for the user's conditions (h = 0.09 mm, t = 0.03 mm), the LOF boundary corresponds to approximately P/v ≈ 0.12–0.14 J/mm (VED ≈ 44–52 J/mm³), though this depends on the actual melt-pool geometry at the specific spot size.

Smith et al. (2024) demonstrated that at a constant VED of 85 J/mm³ with a 100 µm spot on a DMP Flex 350, different P/v combinations produced different defect types and amounts, with low-P/low-v builds showing interpass LOF and high-P/high-v builds showing spatter-induced intrapass LOF (smith2025assessingvolumetricenergy pages 5-7, smith2025assessingvolumetricenergy pages 10-11, smith2025assessingvolumetricenergy pages 1-2). This strongly supports the view that **VED is necessary but not sufficient** as a LOF predictor; the geometric criterion using actual melt-pool dimensions is more reliable.

Barrionuevo et al. recommended a VED above **125 J/mm³** for their Concept Laser MLAB (80 µm spot, 30 µm layers), which is significantly higher than Vallejo's 46 J/mm³ lower bound (barrionuevo2024influenceofthe pages 11-14). This discrepancy likely reflects the smaller spot size (deeper, narrower pools) and different hatch spacing. This highlights that the LOF boundary is **machine- and spot-dependent** (weakly to moderately supported as a general principle; the specific numbers are machine-specific).

### 3. Keyhole Porosity Threshold for 316L at 50–130 µm Spots

King et al. (2014, LLNL) established the keyhole transition for 316L at a **normalized enthalpy ΔH/h_s ≈ 30 ± 4** using the definition ΔH/h_s = AP/(h_s √(π D_th v σ³)), where A is absorptivity (~0.4), h_s is the enthalpy at melting, D_th is thermal diffusivity, v is scan speed, and σ is the beam-radius parameter (king2014observationofkeyholemode pages 19-28, king2014observationofkeyholemode pages 15-19). This threshold was validated with **both 52 µm and 130 µm D4σ beams**, confirming that it scales across beam sizes (king2014observationofkeyholemode pages 19-28). The geometric keyhole criterion was **d > w/2** (depth exceeds half-width) (king2014observationofkeyholemode pages 11-15, king2014observationofkeyholemode pages 28-36).

Bertoli (2018, LLNL) derived a theoretical threshold of **ΔH/h_s ≈ 6** based on the energy to reach the boiling point: ΔH/h_s ≥ πT_b/T_m (bertoli2018processstructurepropertiesrelationshipsina pages 50-56, bertoli2018processstructurepropertiesrelationshipsinb pages 50-56). The difference between the theoretical ≈6 and experimental ≈30 reflects that the definitions differ (King's includes additional scaling factors) and that heat losses reduce effective enthalpy delivery.

Sabzi and Rivera-Díaz-del-Castillo (2019) reported that for 316L, normalized enthalpy values **above ~7** (using their definition) corresponded to keyhole formation, while below 7 was pore-free. At 200 W with scan speeds 850–1600 mm/s, pore fractions were 0.4–2.5% under keyhole conditions (sabzi2019defectpreventionin pages 8-10).

Forien et al. (2020, LLNL) identified the conduction-to-keyhole transition at ΔH/h ≈ **7.3** via in-situ pyrometry (forien2020detectingkeyholeporosity pages 14-19).

**Can 370 W at 1350 mm/s with a 130 µm spot keyhole?** Using King's formulation with the user's 130 µm D4σ spot (σ ≈ 32.5 µm), the normalized enthalpy at 370 W and 1350 mm/s evaluates to a value that falls **near or below** the keyhole threshold of 30 ± 4 (king2014observationofkeyholemode pages 19-28). The larger beam distributes energy over a wider area, reducing peak intensity. For comparison, Gordon et al. noted a keyhole threshold surface power density of ~10⁶ W/cm² for Ti-6Al-4V; at 370 W over a 130 µm diameter circle, the irradiance is approximately **2.8 × 10⁶ W/cm²** (gordon2020defectstructureprocess pages 4-5), which could potentially induce keyhole behavior. However, the relatively high scan speed (1350 mm/s) limits the interaction time, reducing the likelihood of deep keyhole formation. Metelkova et al. (2018) showed that positive defocus (larger effective spot) generally retained conduction-mode processing over a wider parameter range (metelkova2018ontheinfluence pages 10-13), and that melt-pool depth was far more sensitive to beam size than width (metelkova2018ontheinfluence pages 6-8).

**Assessment (moderately supported):** The production condition (370 W, 1350 mm/s, 130 µm) likely operates in the **conduction-to-transition regime**, not deep keyhole. Keyhole porosity is more likely at slower scan speeds within the user's range (e.g., P/v > 0.4 J/mm at 130 µm spot). At the 50–70 µm contour spot and 100–120 W, the lower power keeps the system well within conduction mode.

### 4. Porosity and Melt-Pool Scatter / Repeatability

**Measurement repeatability:** Obeidi et al. (2021) reported a pycnometer measurement standard deviation of only **0.0002** (after 10 repeat measurements), with error bars of approximately **0.002** in relative density (obeidi2021comparisonofthe pages 4-6). Thus, the measurement method itself introduces negligible uncertainty.

**Within-condition scatter:** Vallejo et al. reported standard deviations on relative density ranging from **±0.05% to ±1.35%** across different parameter sets. At the optimum (200 W, 800 mm/s), the SD was only ±0.06%, while at suboptimal conditions (e.g., 125 W, 200 mm/s), it reached ±1.35% (vallejo2021processoptimizationand pages 2-4). This suggests that **scatter increases dramatically at marginal parameters** where stochastic defects (spatter, powder distribution irregularities) dominate.

**Spatter-induced variability:** Bateman et al. showed that at the standard 370 W/1350 mm/s condition, baseline porosity was **0.003%** while enhanced-spatter porosity reached **0.98%**—a variation of two orders of magnitude from spatter alone (bateman2025effectsoflpbf pages 18-22). The relative increase from spatter was 115% for standard energy, 22% for low energy, and 48% for high energy.

**Machine-to-machine variability:** Obeidi et al. found that four machines with the same powder and nominal parameters produced densities spanning approximately **93.88–97.67%** (a ~4 percentage-point range), with Aconity and EOS M280 performing best and Concept Laser (nitrogen atmosphere) performing worst (obeidi2021comparisonofthe pages 4-6, obeidi2021comparisonofthe pages 6-8). Contributing factors included build-chamber size, gas flow, recoater design, and gas type (obeidi2021comparisonofthe pages 10-12).

**Implications for the user's comb specimens (weakly supported, extrapolated):** No study was found reporting direct wall-to-wall porosity scatter for thin-wall geometries. However, based on the above data, for well-optimized parameters (VED ~50–100 J/mm³), wall-to-wall porosity differences below **~0.1–0.3 percentage points** may be within normal stochastic scatter, while differences exceeding **~0.5 percentage points** likely reflect a real process-parameter effect. At marginal parameters near the LOF boundary, scatter increases substantially.

### 5. Open Datasets for Comparison

**LLNL Keyhole-Mode Microscopy Dataset** (Ahlquist et al. 2022, DOE OSTI ID 1878448, DOI: 10.2172/1878448): Contains single-track cross-sectional images, melt-pool width, depth, height, contact angles, continuity ratings, and cavity locations/contours from LPBF experiments. CSV/Excel files are indexed by plate and track. Directly relevant for keyhole-mode benchmarking (ahlquist2022keyholemodemicroscopydataset pages 15-21).

**MeltpoolNet** (Akbari et al.): A tabular dataset of metallic AM melt-pool characteristics referenced in multiple ML studies (jabbour2025amultisourcemelt pages 7-10). It aggregates process parameters and melt-pool dimensions across alloys including 316L, though the depth of 316L coverage varies.

**Melt-Pool-Kinetics** (Jabbour et al. 2025, Figshare, DOI: 10.1038/s41597-025-05597-2): A multi-source compilation in HDF5 format with metadata covering AM process, material, laser power, scan speed, beam size, layer thickness, and defect results. A metadata spreadsheet enables filtering for LPBF 316L entries (jabbour2025amultisourcemelt pages 7-10, jabbour2025amultisourcemelt pages 11-12).

**NIST AM-Bench** (2018, 2022, 2025 challenges): Primarily focused on **IN718** and **IN625** single-track and multi-layer builds with carefully controlled melt-pool measurements. The 316L coverage is limited; the benchmark's main value for the user is methodological rather than material-specific (jabbour2025amultisourcemelt pages 11-12).

**Journal supplementary data:** Vallejo et al. (2021) Table 1 contains a full parameter-density matrix for 316L on the SLM 125HL (vallejo2021processoptimizationand pages 2-4). Barrionuevo et al. (2024) Table 1 compiles a literature survey of 316L LPBF parameters and densities across >10 machines (barrionuevo2024influenceofthe pages 2-4). Gordon et al. (2020) provide Ti-6Al-4V defect process maps with XCT-derived porosity data that can serve as a cross-material reference for the Tang criterion (gordon2020defectstructureprocess pages 4-5, gordon2020defectstructureprocess pages 1-2).

### 6. Summary of Key Thresholds and Recommendations

**Lack-of-fusion boundary (316L, 30 µm layers, 0.09 mm hatch, 100–130 µm spot):**
- VED: approximately **40–50 J/mm³** (strongly supported by multiple studies)
- P/v: approximately **0.11–0.14 J/mm** (dependent on spot and hatch)
- Tang criterion: **(H/W)² + (t/D)² < 1**; this requires knowing W and D at each condition

**Keyhole boundary (316L, 130 µm spot):**
- King's normalized enthalpy: **ΔH/h_s ≈ 30 ± 4** (strongly supported, validated at both 52 and 130 µm)
- Geometric criterion: **d/w > 0.5** or depth exceeding half-width
- At 370 W / 1350 mm/s / 130 µm: likely **conduction-to-transition mode**, not deep keyhole (moderately supported)
- Keyhole risk increases at slower speeds (P/v > ~0.4–0.5 J/mm at 130 µm)

**Expected porosity across the user's window (P = 150–370 W, v ≈ 335–2930 mm/s, h = 0.09 mm, t = 30 µm, 130 µm spot):**
- VED range: ~33–204 J/mm³
- At 33–45 J/mm³ (high-v / low-P corner): **>1–8% porosity** from LOF (bateman2025effectsoflpbf pages 6-13)
- At 50–130 J/mm³ (central window): **<0.5% porosity**, potentially <0.1% at optimum (vallejo2021processoptimizationand pages 2-4, bateman2025effectsoflpbf pages 18-22)
- At >130–200 J/mm³ (low-v / high-P corner): porosity may rise to **0.5–2%** from keyhole and overheating effects (bateman2025effectsoflpbf pages 13-18, vallejo2021processoptimizationand pages 16-18)

**Melt-pool depth estimates:** At the production condition (370 W, 1350 mm/s, 130 µm spot), Kamath et al.'s single-track screening targeted **60–120 µm** depth for high-density builds with a 54 µm beam (kamath2014densityofadditivelymanufactured pages 9-13). With the larger 130 µm spot, shallower pools are expected at the same P/v. At slow speeds (e.g., 370 W, 335 mm/s), depths could reach **200+ µm**, potentially entering keyhole territory.

## Porosity, Melt-Pool Depth, and Process Maps for LPBF 316L Stainless Steel: A Literature Benchmark for the Concept Laser M2 Parameter Window

### 1. Published 316L Process Maps and Density Data in the Proposed Window

The most directly comparable published study is the LLNL work by Kamath et al. (2014), who used a **Concept Laser M2** with a D4σ laser spot of **54 µm** (equivalent to Φ(99%) ≈ 81 µm) and 316L powder (CL20ES) at powers of **150–400 W**, 30 µm layers, and scan speeds spanning approximately 1200–2400 mm/s for density pillars (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000012). At 250 W and above, suitable scan speeds produced **>99% relative density**; at 400 W over 1900–2200 mm/s, density reached approximately **99.5%** (pqac-00000008). Density fell sharply at excessive speed (insufficient melting/LOF) and more gradually at low speed as keyhole voids formed (pqac-00000013). Single-track screening on the same M2 targeted melt-pool depths of **60–120 µm** (approximately 2–3× the 30 µm layer thickness) for high-density builds; the largest measured single-track depth was **195 µm** at 200 W and 500 mm/s (pqac-00000010). Note that the Kamath beam (54 µm D4σ) is considerably smaller than the user's production spot (130 µm), so the energy density at the same P and v is distributed over a larger area in the user's case, reducing penetration depth and shifting the keyhole and LOF boundaries.

Bateman et al. (2025) provide the **closest match to the user's exact machine and production parameters**: a GE Concept M2 with gas-atomized 316L (19–47 µm). Their standard/production condition used **370 W, 1350 mm/s, 90 µm hatch, 50 µm layer, and a 130 µm spot** (VED = 60.9 J/mm³), yielding porosity of **0.003–0.98%** across baseline and enhanced-spatter specimens (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043). Their low-energy condition (290 W, 1200 mm/s, 150 µm hatch, 50 µm layer, 50 µm spot; VED = 32.2 J/mm³) produced **5.85–8.60% porosity**, dominated by lack-of-fusion defects (pqac-00000041). Their high-energy condition (290 W, 800 mm/s, 70 µm hatch, 50 µm layer, 125 µm spot; VED = 103.6 J/mm³) yielded **0.55–1.82% porosity**, with both keyhole and LOF features reported (pqac-00000042). This demonstrates that even at higher VED, density did not necessarily improve, consistent with the onset of keyhole porosity.

Vallejo et al. (2021) used an **SLM 125HL** (≈70 µm spot, 100 °C preheat, argon, 30 µm layers, 120 µm hatch). Their optimized condition was **200 W, 800 mm/s** (VED = 69 J/mm³), achieving **99.89 ± 0.06% relative density**. The dense window spanned **46–127 J/mm³**, with ≥99.8% density throughout (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003). At 200 W, densities across scan speeds of 600–1400 mm/s were 99.92, 99.89, 99.88, 99.83, and 99.44%, respectively, illustrating the LOF edge near 40 J/mm³ (pqac-00000000). Melt-pool widths ranged from ~50–300 µm and depths from ~30–600 µm across all conditions (pqac-00000068).

Barrionuevo et al. (2024) used a **Concept Laser MLAB 200R** (≈80 µm spot, nitrogen, 30 µm layers) with 120–160 W and 700–1100 mm/s. The best densification was **98.3%** (Archimedes) or **99.70%** (image analysis) at 160 W, 700 mm/s, 40 µm hatch (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000044). At a supplementary 180 W point, density reached **99.41 ± 0.23%**; above 180 W, density fell below 98% due to overheating (pqac-00000007).

Yusuf et al. (2017) reported **Concept Laser M2** results at 200 W, 1600 mm/s, 50 µm layers: Archimedes density ≥99%, mean porosity ≈0.82%, XCT maximum porosity ≈0.61%, with spatially non-uniform pore distribution (pqac-00000051).

### 2. Lack-of-Fusion Boundary

**Tang et al.'s geometric overlap criterion** is the most widely used LOF predictor. It models the melt pool as a half-ellipse and requires that adjacent tracks and layers overlap sufficiently. The criterion is expressed as **(H/W)² + (t/D)² ≤ 1**, where H is hatch spacing, W is melt-pool width, t is layer thickness, and D is melt-pool depth (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000026). When this sum exceeds unity, lack-of-fusion porosity is predicted. An alternative linear form, **t/D + H/W ≤ 1**, has also been used (pqac-00000023). Gordon et al. (2020) applied this criterion in Ti-6Al-4V defect structure process maps and noted that VED alone is not a robust LOF predictor because different H and t combinations at the same VED produce different overlap (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000063).

**In VED terms**, the LOF boundary for 316L at 30 µm layers and typical hatch spacings falls at approximately **40–50 J/mm³** (strongly supported). Vallejo et al. found ≥99.8% density for 46–127 J/mm³ (pqac-00000006), and density dropped to 99.44% at 39.7 J/mm³ and further at lower VED. Bateman et al.'s 32.2 J/mm³ condition (with a larger 150 µm hatch and 50 µm spot) produced 5.85–8.60% porosity (pqac-00000041), confirming that the LOF boundary is **sharp**: porosity can rise from <0.5% to >5% over a relatively narrow VED range once the melt pool no longer spans the hatch spacing or layer thickness.

**In P/v terms**, for the user's conditions (h = 0.09 mm, t = 0.03 mm), the LOF boundary corresponds to approximately P/v ≈ 0.12–0.14 J/mm (VED ≈ 44–52 J/mm³), though this depends on the actual melt-pool geometry at the specific spot size.

Smith et al. (2024) demonstrated that at a constant VED of 85 J/mm³ with a 100 µm spot on a DMP Flex 350, different P/v combinations produced different defect types and amounts, with low-P/low-v builds showing interpass LOF and high-P/high-v builds showing spatter-induced intrapass LOF (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048). This strongly supports the view that **VED is necessary but not sufficient** as a LOF predictor; the geometric criterion using actual melt-pool dimensions is more reliable.

Barrionuevo et al. recommended a VED above **125 J/mm³** for their Concept Laser MLAB (80 µm spot, 30 µm layers), which is significantly higher than Vallejo's 46 J/mm³ lower bound (pqac-00000007). This discrepancy likely reflects the smaller spot size (deeper, narrower pools) and different hatch spacing. This highlights that the LOF boundary is **machine- and spot-dependent** (weakly to moderately supported as a general principle; the specific numbers are machine-specific).

### 3. Keyhole Porosity Threshold for 316L at 50–130 µm Spots

King et al. (2014, LLNL) established the keyhole transition for 316L at a **normalized enthalpy ΔH/h_s ≈ 30 ± 4** using the definition ΔH/h_s = AP/(h_s √(π D_th v σ³)), where A is absorptivity (~0.4), h_s is the enthalpy at melting, D_th is thermal diffusivity, v is scan speed, and σ is the beam-radius parameter (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015). This threshold was validated with **both 52 µm and 130 µm D4σ beams**, confirming that it scales across beam sizes (pqac-00000059). The geometric keyhole criterion was **d > w/2** (depth exceeds half-width) (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000034).

Bertoli (2018, LLNL) derived a theoretical threshold of **ΔH/h_s ≈ 6** based on the energy to reach the boiling point: ΔH/h_s ≥ πT_b/T_m (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017). The difference between the theoretical ≈6 and experimental ≈30 reflects that the definitions differ (King's includes additional scaling factors) and that heat losses reduce effective enthalpy delivery.

Sabzi and Rivera-Díaz-del-Castillo (2019) reported that for 316L, normalized enthalpy values **above ~7** (using their definition) corresponded to keyhole formation, while below 7 was pore-free. At 200 W with scan speeds 850–1600 mm/s, pore fractions were 0.4–2.5% under keyhole conditions (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000057).

Forien et al. (2020, LLNL) identified the conduction-to-keyhole transition at ΔH/h ≈ **7.3** via in-situ pyrometry (pqac-00000018).

**Can 370 W at 1350 mm/s with a 130 µm spot keyhole?** Using King's formulation with the user's 130 µm D4σ spot (σ ≈ 32.5 µm), the normalized enthalpy at 370 W and 1350 mm/s evaluates to a value that falls **near or below** the keyhole threshold of 30 ± 4 (pqac-00000059). The larger beam distributes energy over a wider area, reducing peak intensity. For comparison, Gordon et al. noted a keyhole threshold surface power density of ~10⁶ W/cm² for Ti-6Al-4V; at 370 W over a 130 µm diameter circle, the irradiance is approximately **2.8 × 10⁶ W/cm²** (pqac-00000058), which could potentially induce keyhole behavior. However, the relatively high scan speed (1350 mm/s) limits the interaction time, reducing the likelihood of deep keyhole formation. Metelkova et al. (2018) showed that positive defocus (larger effective spot) generally retained conduction-mode processing over a wider parameter range (pqac-00000065), and that melt-pool depth was far more sensitive to beam size than width (pqac-00000064).

**Assessment (moderately supported):** The production condition (370 W, 1350 mm/s, 130 µm) likely operates in the **conduction-to-transition regime**, not deep keyhole. Keyhole porosity is more likely at slower scan speeds within the user's range (e.g., P/v > 0.4 J/mm at 130 µm spot). At the 50–70 µm contour spot and 100–120 W, the lower power keeps the system well within conduction mode.

### 4. Porosity and Melt-Pool Scatter / Repeatability

**Measurement repeatability:** Obeidi et al. (2021) reported a pycnometer measurement standard deviation of only **0.0002** (after 10 repeat measurements), with error bars of approximately **0.002** in relative density (pqac-00000050). Thus, the measurement method itself introduces negligible uncertainty.

**Within-condition scatter:** Vallejo et al. reported standard deviations on relative density ranging from **±0.05% to ±1.35%** across different parameter sets. At the optimum (200 W, 800 mm/s), the SD was only ±0.06%, while at suboptimal conditions (e.g., 125 W, 200 mm/s), it reached ±1.35% (pqac-00000000). This suggests that **scatter increases dramatically at marginal parameters** where stochastic defects (spatter, powder distribution irregularities) dominate.

**Spatter-induced variability:** Bateman et al. showed that at the standard 370 W/1350 mm/s condition, baseline porosity was **0.003%** while enhanced-spatter porosity reached **0.98%**—a variation of two orders of magnitude from spatter alone (pqac-00000040). The relative increase from spatter was 115% for standard energy, 22% for low energy, and 48% for high energy.

**Machine-to-machine variability:** Obeidi et al. found that four machines with the same powder and nominal parameters produced densities spanning approximately **93.88–97.67%** (a ~4 percentage-point range), with Aconity and EOS M280 performing best and Concept Laser (nitrogen atmosphere) performing worst (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000054). Contributing factors included build-chamber size, gas flow, recoater design, and gas type (pqac-00000053).

**Implications for the user's comb specimens (weakly supported, extrapolated):** No study was found reporting direct wall-to-wall porosity scatter for thin-wall geometries. However, based on the above data, for well-optimized parameters (VED ~50–100 J/mm³), wall-to-wall porosity differences below **~0.1–0.3 percentage points** may be within normal stochastic scatter, while differences exceeding **~0.5 percentage points** likely reflect a real process-parameter effect. At marginal parameters near the LOF boundary, scatter increases substantially.

### 5. Open Datasets for Comparison

**LLNL Keyhole-Mode Microscopy Dataset** (Ahlquist et al. 2022, DOE OSTI ID 1878448, DOI: 10.2172/1878448): Contains single-track cross-sectional images, melt-pool width, depth, height, contact angles, continuity ratings, and cavity locations/contours from LPBF experiments. CSV/Excel files are indexed by plate and track. Directly relevant for keyhole-mode benchmarking (pqac-00000029).

**MeltpoolNet** (Akbari et al.): A tabular dataset of metallic AM melt-pool characteristics referenced in multiple ML studies (pqac-00000030). It aggregates process parameters and melt-pool dimensions across alloys including 316L, though the depth of 316L coverage varies.

**Melt-Pool-Kinetics** (Jabbour et al. 2025, Figshare, DOI: 10.1038/s41597-025-05597-2): A multi-source compilation in HDF5 format with metadata covering AM process, material, laser power, scan speed, beam size, layer thickness, and defect results. A metadata spreadsheet enables filtering for LPBF 316L entries (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031).

**NIST AM-Bench** (2018, 2022, 2025 challenges): Primarily focused on **IN718** and **IN625** single-track and multi-layer builds with carefully controlled melt-pool measurements. The 316L coverage is limited; the benchmark's main value for the user is methodological rather than material-specific (pqac-00000031).

**Journal supplementary data:** Vallejo et al. (2021) Table 1 contains a full parameter-density matrix for 316L on the SLM 125HL (pqac-00000000). Barrionuevo et al. (2024) Table 1 compiles a literature survey of 316L LPBF parameters and densities across >10 machines (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000049). Gordon et al. (2020) provide Ti-6Al-4V defect process maps with XCT-derived porosity data that can serve as a cross-material reference for the Tang criterion (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000063).

### 6. Summary of Key Thresholds and Recommendations

**Lack-of-fusion boundary (316L, 30 µm layers, 0.09 mm hatch, 100–130 µm spot):**
- VED: approximately **40–50 J/mm³** (strongly supported by multiple studies)
- P/v: approximately **0.11–0.14 J/mm** (dependent on spot and hatch)
- Tang criterion: **(H/W)² + (t/D)² < 1**; this requires knowing W and D at each condition

**Keyhole boundary (316L, 130 µm spot):**
- King's normalized enthalpy: **ΔH/h_s ≈ 30 ± 4** (strongly supported, validated at both 52 and 130 µm)
- Geometric criterion: **d/w > 0.5** or depth exceeding half-width
- At 370 W / 1350 mm/s / 130 µm: likely **conduction-to-transition mode**, not deep keyhole (moderately supported)
- Keyhole risk increases at slower speeds (P/v > ~0.4–0.5 J/mm at 130 µm)

**Expected porosity across the user's window (P = 150–370 W, v ≈ 335–2930 mm/s, h = 0.09 mm, t = 30 µm, 130 µm spot):**
- VED range: ~33–204 J/mm³
- At 33–45 J/mm³ (high-v / low-P corner): **>1–8% porosity** from LOF (pqac-00000041)
- At 50–130 J/mm³ (central window): **<0.5% porosity**, potentially <0.1% at optimum (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000040)
- At >130–200 J/mm³ (low-v / high-P corner): porosity may rise to **0.5–2%** from keyhole and overheating effects (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000006)

**Melt-pool depth estimates:** At the production condition (370 W, 1350 mm/s, 130 µm spot), Kamath et al.'s single-track screening targeted **60–120 µm** depth for high-density builds with a 54 µm beam (pqac-00000010). With the larger 130 µm spot, shallower pools are expected at the same P/v. At slow speeds (e.g., 370 W, 335 mm/s), depths could reach **200+ µm**, potentially entering keyhole territory.

contexts.context: The 316L stainless-steel LPBF parts were fabricated on a Concept Laser MLAB 200R using a 200 W Nd:YAG fiber laser with a focused spot diameter of approximately 80 µm and a 1070 nm wavelength. The study used laser powers of 120, 140, and 160 W; scan speeds of 700, 900, and 1100 mm/s; hatch spacings of 40, 60, and 80 µm; and a constant 30 µm layer thickness. The chamber was nitrogen-filled, with oxygen below 800 ppm. Density was measured by Archimedes’ principle, while porosity was evaluated from optical and SEM images. The highest measured overall densification was 98.3% at 160 W, 700 mm/s, and 40 µm hatch spacing. Average relative density decreased as scan speed increased: 96.29 ± 1.02% at 700 mm/s, 94.62 ± 1.24% at 900 mm/s, and 93.64 ± 1.55% at 1100 mm/s. At fixed 160 W and 40 µm hatch spacing, image-analysis relative densities were 96.68%, 97.41%, and 99.70% for 1100, 900, and 700 mm/s, respectively. The excerpt also identifies optical microscopy, SEM/EDS, GDOES, a roughness tester, and a Vickers hardness tester as characterization equipment.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides several LPBF parameter and density findings for 316L stainless steel, but it does not identify the LPBF machine, powder-bed machine model, nominal laser spot size, or a complete parameter-by-parameter density table. Laser scanning speeds above 700 mm/s caused incomplete melting and lack-of-fusion defects. A volumetric energy density (VED) below 100 J/mm3 generated irregular porosity, while a VED above 125 J/mm3 was recommended for proper powder fusion. The study used 160 W as its maximum standard laser power, while supplementary testing found that 180 W increased relative density to 99.41 ± 0.23%; powers above 180 W caused overheating and reduced density to below 98%. Hatch spacing was evaluated at least at 40 and 60 µm; their density difference was minimal, and 60 µm was recommended because smaller hatch spacing increases production time. The stated layer thickness was approximately 30 µm. For suitable molten-pool geometry, penetration depth should be 50–80 µm, and the molten-pool width should not be below the 100 µm laser focus. Typical spherical pores had an average diameter below 9 ± 2 µm. Specific density values for the other individual power, speed, and hatch combinations, as well as machine details, are not included in this excerpt.
